claims.claim: Two linked papers on global health threats appear in the current issue of The Lancet, one from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation.
claims.episode_span: Two linked papers examine major risks to human survival and health systems through the rest of the century. One provides the main analysis from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation.
claims.source_title: Just published in The Lancet: Global threats to health in the 21st century
claims.supporting_quote: Just published @TheLancet Global threats to health in the 21st century an opus, 59 page comprehensive dissection of all the threats we face

claims.claim: Genome editing was used by two independent teams to record cell divisions from zygote to organ formation, with results in Science and Cell.
claims.episode_span: Two independent teams used genome editing to record every division from zygote through organ formation. One study appears in Science and the other in Cell.
claims.source_title: Genome editing traces mammalian embryo development in detail
claims.supporting_quote: When genome editing got going, the ability to trace a mammalian embryo's development to organ generation in exquisite detail was not envisioned. Now it's been accomplished by 2 independent groups.

claims.claim: Florida Tech researchers found low-oxygen zones release phosphorus and nitrogen that support algal blooms in the Banana River.
claims.episode_span: Low-oxygen zones on the river floor cause phosphorus and nitrogen to re-enter the water column. These nutrients directly support harmful algal growth.
claims.source_title: New study shows effects of hypoxia in Florida's Banana River
claims.supporting_quote: A new study by Florida Tech assistant professor of marine sciences Austin Fox, Ph.D. '15, found that low oxygen levels are contributing to the rerelease of nutrients buried on the river floor that feed harmful algal blooms.

claims.claim: A Jurassic fossil shows jaw and throat bones already possessed the anatomy for suckling 165 million years ago, according to findings in Nature.
claims.episode_span: Key jaw and throat bones already show the anatomy needed for suckling, swallowing, and milk consumption. The structures predate the appearance of crown-group mammals by tens of millions of years. The findings appear in Nature.
claims.source_title: Jurassic fossil reveals ancient origins of how mammals drink milk
claims.supporting_quote: Their findings, published in Nature, suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals.

claims.claim: Chinese researchers packaged photosynthetic machinery from spinach into nanoparticles that generated ATP in rat heart cells under light.
claims.episode_span: Researchers in China extracted photosynthetic machinery from spinach leaves and packaged it into nanoparticles. When introduced into cultured rat heart cells, the particles generated ATP under light exposure.
claims.source_title: Spinach nanoparticles help failing rat hearts via 'borrowed photosynthesis'
claims.supporting_quote: Researchers in China have brought part of the leaf's energy-making machinery into rat heart cells to test whether borrowed photosynthesis could help an overworked heart.

claims.claim: NYU Abu Dhabi researchers developed an algorithm that predicts Arctic sea-ice extent up to nine months ahead, published in Scientific Reports.
claims.episode_span: Scientists at NYU Abu Dhabi’s ACCESS center built a model that predicts sea-ice extent up to nine months in advance. The algorithm improves on earlier statistical approaches by incorporating additional physical variables. Output appears in Scientific Reports.
claims.source_title: New algorithm could predict Arctic sea ice up to 9 months ahead, offering new climate insights
claims.supporting_quote: Researchers at the Mubadala Arabian Center for Climate and Environmental Sciences (ACCESS) at NYU Abu Dhabi have developed a new algorithm that can forecast Arctic sea ice extent up to nine months in advance, offering a new way to anticipate changes in the Arctic that can affect the global climate system. The research is published in the journal Scientific Reports.
